chapters.title: Chapter 1: What an Economic Moat Really Is

lessons.title: Why Some Companies Keep Earning High Returns: The Idea of a Moat

body.text: High profits attract competitors, and competitors destroy high profits. An economic moat is whatever stops that from happening.

children.text: Every business that earns unusually high returns sends out an invitation. Rivals notice the fat margins, raise capital, copy the product, cut prices, and poach the customers. Over time, returns get dragged down towards the minimum investors will accept. This is not a theory, it is the default outcome for most companies listed on the NSE and BSE.

And yet a handful of businesses keep earning high returns for ten, twenty, even thirty years, while well-funded competitors throw money at the same market. Understanding why is the single most useful question a long-term equity investor can ask.
The Castle and the Moat

markDefs.definition: A durable structural advantage that protects a company's high returns on capital from competition for many years.

children.text: Warren Buffett popularised the idea. Think of a profitable business as a castle full of gold. Competitors are the armies outside, and they want in. A
moat

is the structural feature that keeps them out: a brand customers will pay extra for, a network that gets stronger with every user, a cost structure rivals cannot match, or a licence nobody else can get.

markDefs.definition: Operating profit (EBIT) divided by capital employed (equity plus debt). It measures how much profit a business generates on every rupee invested in it.
The minimum return investors and lenders demand for funding a business, given its risk. For most Indian listed companies it is commonly estimated at roughly 11% to 13%.

children.text: Morningstar later organised moats into five sources, and this course follows that framework. But first, you need to see what a moat looks like in the numbers, because the financial fingerprint is the same regardless of the source. That fingerprint is
return on capital employed (ROCE)
that stays above the
cost of capital
year after year.

body.title: Illustrative: ROCE of a Moat Business vs a No-Moat Business

children.text: Both businesses start in the same place. The difference is what happens after competitors show up. The no-moat business watches its returns slide to the cost of capital within five or six years. It still exists, it still grows revenue, but it no longer creates any value above what an investor could earn elsewhere at the same risk. The moat business absorbs the same competitive pressure and keeps its returns intact.

body.text: The useful question is never "how profitable is this company today?" It is "why hasn't competition already killed these profits, and will that reason still hold ten years from now?"

children.text: Two Indian Industries, Two Very Different Outcomes

Indian aviation is the textbook no-moat industry. Passenger traffic has grown enormously over two decades, yet the list of casualties is long: Kingfisher Airlines stopped flying in 2012, Jet Airways was grounded in April 2019, and Go First filed for insolvency in May 2023. Seats are nearly identical across airlines, customers book on price through aggregators, and a new entrant can lease aircraft.
Growth without a moat transferred value to passengers, not shareholders.

Decorative paints tell the opposite story. Asian Paints has earned returns on capital far above its cost of capital for decades. Its brand, its tinting-machine network in dealer shops, and a supply chain that restocks tens of thousands of dealers quickly are hard to replicate. That moat is now being tested by well-funded entrants, including Grasim's Birla Opus, launched in 2024, and Chapter 6 of this course looks at exactly that kind of challenge.

body.title: What Competition Does to Each Type of Business

columns.label: Without a moat
points: New entrants copy the product quickly
Price becomes the main way to win customers
Margins and ROCE fall towards the cost of capital
Revenue growth needs ever more capital
Shareholders earn little above a fixed deposit adjusted for risk

columns.label: With a moat
points: Entrants struggle to win customers even at lower prices
The company can raise prices without losing volume
ROCE stays well above the cost of capital for years
Growth is funded largely from internal cash flows
Profits compound for shareholders over long periods

children.text: The Five Sources of a Moat
Each chapter from 2 to 4 goes deep into these. For now, just learn to recognise them.

body.caption: The five moat sources with Indian listed examples

cells: Brands, patents, or licences let a company charge more or keep rivals out entirely
Asian Paints (brand and dealer trust), CRISIL (regulated rating licence plus reputation)
Leaving is expensive, risky, or painful for the customer, so they stay
TCS and Infosys (client systems deeply embedded in operations)
Each new user makes the product more valuable for every other user
Info Edge (more recruiters on Naukri attract more jobseekers, and vice versa)
The company can sell profitably at prices rivals cannot survive at
Avenue Supermarts, DMart (owned stores, tight costs, everyday low prices)
The market is only big enough for one or two players to earn good returns
CDSL (one of only two depositories in India, alongside NSDL)

body.label: The moat test in one line
body.value: ROCE above the cost of capital, sustained through competition, for 10+ years
body.context: The numbers are the evidence. The business reason (one of the five sources) must explain them.

children.text: Why This Matters for Your Returns

A moat does not just protect today's profit. It protects the rate at which future profits grow. A company can only grow earnings as fast as it can reinvest profits at a good return, and a moat is what keeps that return high.

body.caption: Sustainable growth in earnings, assuming returns on new capital match existing ROCE

children.text: Take two companies, each with ₹100 crore of capital, each reinvesting 60% of profits back into the business. Company A has a moat and earns 25% ROCE. Company B has none and earns 12%, right at its cost of capital.

Same starting capital, same reinvestment discipline. After a decade, Company A earns more than four times what Company B earns. That gap, not a clever entry price, is where most long-term wealth in Indian equities has been made.
Company A: starting profit = 25% of ₹100 crore = ₹25 crore. After ten years of 15% growth: ₹25 crore × 1.15^10 = ₹25 crore × 4.046 ≈ ₹101 crore.
Company B: starting profit = 12% of ₹100 crore = ₹12 crore. After ten years of 7.2% growth: ₹12 crore × 1.072^10 = ₹12 crore × 2.004 ≈ ₹24 crore.
The ratio is roughly 101 ÷ 24 ≈ 4.2 times. Starting profits differed by about 2.1 times, and ten years of faster compounding doubled that gap.

body.title: Calculate Sustainable Growth
body.prompt: A company earns a steady ROCE of 20% and reinvests 50% of its profits back into the business at that same return. What is its sustainable earnings growth rate?
body.explanation: g = ROCE × Reinvestment Rate = 20% × 0.50 = 10%. If competition pushed its ROCE down to 12% with the same reinvestment, growth would fall to 6%.

body.title: Spot the Moat Evidence
body.question: Which of these is the strongest evidence that a company has an economic moat?
options: The share price doubled in the last 12 months
ROCE stayed above 20% for ten years even as new competitors entered
It is the most recognised brand in its category
body.explanation: Revenue growth and share price moves say nothing about whether returns can be defended. A famous brand may or may not translate into pricing power. Sustained high ROCE through a period of real competition is the evidence that something is actually protecting profits.

body.title: Is This a Moat or a Head Start?
body.scenario: A listed Indian consumer fintech has reported ROCE of 35% for the last two years. Revenue is growing fast and the stock trades at 70 times earnings. Over the same period, three venture-funded rivals and one large private bank have launched near-identical apps, and all four are offering cashback to win users.
body.prompt: Does two years of 35% ROCE prove this company has a moat? What would you want to see before concluding it does?
body.modelAnswer: No. Two years is too short, and the high returns were earned before serious competition arrived, so they have not been tested. The cashback war is exactly the kind of pressure that pushes no-moat returns down. Before calling it a moat, you would want to see: ROCE holding up (not just revenue growing) after the rivals scale; customers staying even when competitors offer better cashback, which suggests switching costs or network effects; the company not being forced to match rival pricing; and a clear business reason from the five sources that explains why a large bank with a bigger balance sheet cannot simply replicate it. Until then, this looks like a head start, and a 70 times earnings valuation is pricing in a moat that has not been proven. Remember what happened to incumbent telecom returns when Jio entered in 2016.

cards.definition: A durable structural advantage that lets a company keep earning returns above its cost of capital despite competition.
Return on capital employed: EBIT ÷ (equity + debt). The core number for spotting a moat.
The minimum return investors and lenders require. Returns below it destroy value, returns above it create value.
The tendency of unusually high returns to fall back towards the cost of capital as competition arrives.
ROCE × reinvestment rate. How fast earnings can grow from internally generated profits.

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: Open any company page and scroll to the Ratios section to see ROCE for the last 10+ years. Try Asian Paints, then an airline stock, and compare the pattern.

body.title: Your First Moat Check on Screener.in
steps: Pick three companies you own directly or through a mutual fund
On screener.in, find the ROCE % row in the Ratios section for each
Count how many of the last 10 years ROCE was above 15% (a conservative stand-in for cost of capital plus a margin of safety)
For any company that clears 8 out of 10 years, write one sentence on why you think competitors have not been able to bring those returns down
If you cannot write that sentence, note it. That gap is what the rest of this course will help you fill

body.text: Companies named in this lesson are used purely to illustrate concepts. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security. The ROCE chart is illustrative, not the actual data of any company.

points: In a competitive market, high returns attract rivals, and rivals push returns down towards the cost of capital
An economic moat is the structural reason a company can keep earning high returns despite that pressure
The financial fingerprint of a moat is ROCE staying above the cost of capital for 10+ years, through real competition
The five moat sources are intangible assets, switching costs, network effects, cost advantages, and efficient scale
Growth without a moat, as Indian aviation shows, can transfer value to customers rather than shareholders
Sustainable growth = ROCE × reinvestment rate, which is why a moat protects not just today's profit but the pace of future compounding
